normalizedClaims.claimText: The kelvin, symbol K, is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature -- distinct from a practical temperature scale such as Celsius, which has an arbitrary zero point.

The unit of Celsius temperature, the degree Celsius (°C), is by definition equal in magnitude to the kelvin. Celsius temperature t and thermodynamic temperature T (in kelvin) are related by t = T − 273.15 (equivalently T = t + 273.15), where 273.15 is the fixed offset between the two scales' zero points.

normalizedClaims.claimText: In AT&T Bell System subscriber telephone sets, the ringer is standardly provided as an integral paired combination with a dedicated capacitor -- for example, the 531A high-impedance extension-ringer set 'consists of a B-type ringer and an 0.5-uf capacitor', and the internal assembly of the 685-, 686-, 687-, and 690-type subscriber sets wires a 198C capacitor directly to the C4A ringer.

In UK telephone wiring, an incoming call is signalled by the exchange applying a large AC ringing-current voltage (about 80V) to the line. In order to separate this ringing current from the rest of the telephone circuit, a bell capacitor is used to route the ringing current to the bell (the capacitor is connected at one end to a line wire and at the other end to the bell/ringer, the ringer's other connection going to the other line wire). This establishes the capacitor's causal role as routing/separating the AC ringing signal into the ringer circuit, distinct from the ringer-capacitor component pairing alone.

results.reviewNote: Repair: the Project Architect flagged that Bell System Practices confirms the ringer+capacitor pairing but not the capacitor's causal role. A second source (Andrews & Arnold's UK telecoms technical documentation) states the causal function directly: the capacitor routes/separates the AC ringing current to the bell. The two sources describe two distinct national telephony wiring traditions (US Bell System internal subscriber-set wiring vs UK external bell-wire/master-socket wiring); both are cited only for the general functional principle they each individually state, not merged into a single claimed circuit topology.
